text:
The barcodes on the organic honeycrisp apples had always given Nora trouble. The glossy skin refused to hold the sticker flat, so when she passed the fruit over the crimson scanner at Lane 4, the machine remained stubbornly silent. She would have to punch the PLU code—3283—into a keypad covered in yellowing plastic, punctured at the seven and the zero by the acrylic nails of whoever had worked the shift before her.

For four years, her existence had been metered by that high-pitched beep, a sound so pervasive she sometimes heard it in her studio apartment while trying to sleep. Even now, six months after untying her green polyester apron for the last time, her right arm occasionally twitched with the phantom memory of sliding a half-gallon of milk across brushed steel.

Her fingers, at present, rested not on vulcanized rubber, but on a slab of gray-veined Calacatta marble in her mother-in-law’s breakfast room in Bronxville.

"You have good hands, Nora," Miss Emily said, not looking up from the *Financial Times* folded beside her bone-china coffee cup. "Long fingers. Though you do something peculiar with your thumbs when you’re idle. You tuck them in. Like a bird hiding its head."

Nora immediately flattened her palms against the cold stone. "It’s from the register," she said before she could stop herself. Julian had told her, in his gentle, evasive way, that there was no need to constantly refer to the Stop & Shop, as though it were a war she had fought in. *You’re here now,* he’d said, kissing the bridge of her nose. *Let it go.*

Miss Emily turned a page. The salmon-colored paper made a dry, crisp sound. "Well," she said mildly. "We must find them something else to remember."

Nobody called her Emily—not the men who came on Tuesdays to clip the boxwoods, and certainly not Julian, who had spent most of his thirty-two years referring to his mother in the third person. She was "Miss Emily," a designation begun thirty years ago at the boutique investment firm she co-founded in Midtown, when the secretaries settled on an honorific suggesting both gentility and absolute authority. Her husband, a mild-mannered professor of numismatics at Columbia, had died when Julian was twelve, leaving behind a formidable collection of Byzantine bronze coins and very little else in the way of genetic assertion.

Julian had met Nora in November, during a nor’easter that knocked out the power grid. He had wandered into the Stop & Shop on Saw Mill River Road looking for batteries and tonic water, wearing a Barbour jacket that smelled like wet dog. The backup generators were humming, casting the aisles in an emergency-lighting gloom, and Nora was the only cashier left. When he handed her a twenty-dollar bill for D-cells and a bruised lime, their fingers brushed. He looked at her with the sudden, terrifying focus of a man who had spent six years working on a monograph about nineteenth-century agrarian land reform and had forgotten what a woman’s collarbone looked like under fluorescent bulbs.

He came back the next day for paper towels. On Friday, it was olive oil. By February, they were married in the office of a town clerk in White Plains.

It had happened with the weightless momentum of a dream. Julian was not a rebellious man, and it took Nora three weeks of marriage to understand that she was not his rebellion, either. Rather, she was his refuge. He loved her because she did not care about the yield curve, because she found his stories about nineteenth-century tenant farmers genuinely sad, and because she smelled of dry laundry sheets and cinnamon gum rather than the sharp ozone of Miss Emily’s expectations.

Miss Emily had not been informed of the wedding until three days after the fact. They drove up the gravel driveway of the Bronxville house—a sprawling Tudor Revival constructed to withstand a siege—in Julian’s aging Volvo. Nora wore a navy-blue dress from Marshall’s, expecting shouting, or at least to be offered a check to disappear, like in the paperbacks she read between customers.

Instead, Miss Emily stood in the foyer in cream-colored wool trousers, her silver hair cut in a blunt, architectural bob. She looked at Julian’s left hand, then at Nora’s, and then at Nora’s imitation suede shoes.

"February is a dreadful month for an anniversary," Miss Emily had said, turning toward the drawing room. "Nothing is in season. Come in. Maria has just made a pot of Darjeeling, though if we’re celebrating, I suppose we ought to open the Billecart-Salmon. Julian, go down to the cellar."

And that had been that. Nora was absorbed.

It was not rejection that Nora found difficult to navigate in the months that followed; it was the relentless mechanics of Miss Emily’s acceptance. A rejection would have had edges she could push against, retreating with Julian to his book-cluttered apartment in Riverdale to play the wronged working-class wife. Instead, Miss Emily treated her like an underperforming subsidiary acquired in a hostile takeover that required a thorough restructuring before the next quarterly report.

"Julian tells me you have no people," Miss Emily remarked that morning in the breakfast room, setting the newspaper aside.

"My mother lives in Sarasota," Nora said, looking out the leaded-glass window at the lawn. "With her second husband. He sells marine insurance."

"Yes, that’s what I meant," Miss Emily said, not unkindly. "It’s cleaner that way, isn't it? In-laws are so often a clutter. You, at least, arrive unencumbered."

"I have a collection of depression glass," Nora said, a stubborn heat rising in her neck. "Green. My grandmother left it to me."

Miss Emily looked at her across the expanse of marble. Her eyes were a very pale, clear gray, like water at the bottom of a quarry. "Depression glass," she repeated. "Yes. They gave it away in boxes of detergent, didn't they? It has a certain sociological charm. We must put a piece or two on the sideboard in the Riverdale apartment. Julian has no eye for objects. He lives entirely in his head, like his father."

Julian entered the room then, wearing a flannel shirt that had lost a button at the cuff. He looked younger here, in his mother’s house. His shoulders rounded slightly; his voice dropped into a more tentative register.

"What are we putting on the sideboard?" he asked, kissing the top of Nora’s head and brushing his cheek against his mother’s temple.

"Nora’s heirlooms," Miss Emily said briskly. "And we are going into town after breakfast. Nora needs a coat for the Peabody dinner on Thursday. The thing she arrived in yesterday looks as though it were quilted from sleeping bags."

"It’s Lands’ End," Nora said. "It’s rated for twenty below."

"The Peabody dinner is at the University Club, darling, not the Yukon," Miss Emily said, rising from the table. "And Julian, do something about your cuff. You look like a refugee from a Chekhov play."

The town car was waiting at ten. On the drive down the Henry Hudson Parkway, Miss Emily sat in the back with Nora, her Hermès agenda open on her lap, making small, lethal checkmarks with a gold pen.

Nora looked out the tinted window at the lead-colored river. Six months ago on a Saturday morning, she would have been standing on the black rubber mat at Lane 4, her lower back aching, watching the conveyor belt bring her a tide of human sustenance and folly: thirty-six-packs of Diet Coke, generic margarine, ground chuck weeping pink fluid into styrofoam trays. You learned things about people from what they bought. You learned who was lonely by the single-serving frozen lasagnas; you learned who was desperate by the way they watched the green numbers climb on the display, hands hovering over their purses, ready to say, *Put the grapes back, actually, I don't need the grapes.*

What did Miss Emily’s purchases say about her? So far as Nora could tell, Miss Emily never bought anything in a package. Food simply materialized in the Bronxville kitchen, stripped of commercial origins. Nothing had a price tag, because everything had already been paid for, long ago, by some invisible, frictionless mechanism.

"You’re very quiet," Miss Emily said, clicking her pen shut.

"I was thinking about grapes," Nora said.

Miss Emily nodded, as if grapes were a perfectly reasonable subject for a young bride to contemplate on the way to Bergdorf Goodman. "The red seedless have been dreadful lately. All water and no tannin. Now, on the fourth floor, let me speak to Brenda. If she thinks you’re timid, she will put you in navy blue taffeta and you will look like the wife of a minor state assemblyman from Utica."

Bergdorf’s smelled of lilies, floor wax, and tissue paper. Within ten minutes, Nora was standing in a three-way mirror in her Target cotton underwear while Brenda and Miss Emily studied her reflection with the detached intensity of two butchers evaluating a side of beef.

"She has a waist," Brenda said, sounding mildly surprised.

"Of course she has a waist," Miss Emily said. "She hasn't spent the last decade sitting at Le Bilboquet eating truffle risotto like those girls Julian used to bring around. Look at her shoulders. She’s carried things."

Nora stared at herself in the glass. Between her shoulder blades, she felt a phantom ache—the exact spot that used to seize up when a customer left four forty-pound bags of water-softener salt in the bottom of the cart for her to scan with the handheld gun.

"Here," Brenda said, stepping forward with a dress of heavy, matte silk in a shade between moss and slate. She slipped it over Nora’s head. The fabric was cool and astonishingly heavy; it fell over her, erasing the slight bump of her hipbones, transforming her instantly from a girl who knew the PLU code for loose garlic into a woman who looked as though she owned land in Connecticut.

Nora reached down and touched the hem. Her thumb caught slightly on the silk—a tiny rasp of rough skin from a hangnail.

"Don't fidget," Miss Emily said, stepping into the mirror's frame to adjust the neckline. Her fingers were cool and dry, smelling of lemon verbena. In the glass, their eyes met.

"Julian thinks I’m a monster, you know," Miss Emily said conversationally, as Brenda knelt with a mouthful of pins. "He thinks I’m going to eat you alive. He has a very melodramatic view of me. It comes from reading all those nineteenth-century pamphlets about absentee landlords."

"I don't think you're a monster," Nora said.

"No, I didn't think you did," Miss Emily replied, smoothing the silk over Nora’s shoulder. "That’s why I like you. Those other girls—the ones from Brearley with the hyphenated names—they were terrified of me. It was exhausting. You look at me the way you probably looked at a woman trying to pass an expired coupon."

Nora felt the corner of her mouth twitch. "Only if she was rude about it. If she was nice, I just scanned it anyway and threw it in the drawer."

Miss Emily gave a short, sharp bark of laughter. "Yes," she said, her pale eyes gleaming in the mirror. "I imagined you did. Integrity is all very well, Nora, but discretion is much more useful in the long run. Brenda, we’ll take this one, and the camel coat by the elevators."

They had lunch afterward at a small Italian place on Madison where the tablecloths muffled the sound of the silverware. Miss Emily ordered branzino for both of them and a half-carafe of dry white wine.

"Julian’s book will not be published by Oxford," Miss Emily said, expertly detaching a fillet of fish from its spine. "His advisor called me last week. Arthur and Ronald were at Yale together; of course he calls me. The manuscript is too narrow. It’s four hundred pages on the turnip crop in Shropshire between 1842 and 1848. Nobody wants to read that."

Nora set her wineglass down. "He’s worked on it for six years," she said. "He gets up at five in the morning to work on it before his lectures."

"Effort is not an asset class, darling," Miss Emily said gently. "If it were, the men who dig ditches on the Cross Bronx Expressway would be running the Federal Reserve. Julian is a dear boy, and he has a very sweet nature, which he got from Arthur. But he has no killer instinct. He hides in the archives because the people there are all dead and cannot argue with him."

"He’s happy in the archives," Nora said.

"He is comfortable in the archives," Miss Emily corrected her. "There is a difference. And when Oxford sends the rejection letter next month, he will be devastated, and he will talk about giving up the tenure track and moving to Vermont to teach at a progressive boarding school where they grade the children on their empathy."

Nora looked down at her fish. Julian *had* mentioned Vermont once, late at night, lying in bed while the subway rumbled three blocks away. He had talked about a small college near Bennington, about having a garden. Nora had stroked his thinning hair and thought about how cold Vermont must be in January, and how she had spent her entire life in rooms where the heat was controlled by someone else.

"You don't want to go to Vermont, do you, Nora?" Miss Emily asked softly.

Nora looked up. The older woman was watching her with an expression that was neither cruel nor warm, only terrifyingly clear. It was the look of a person who had audited the ledger of the world and arrived at the exact sum to the penny.

"I've never been to Vermont," Nora said carefully.

"It’s full of damp wood and people who inherited money in the seventies pretending to be carpenters," Miss Emily said, sipping her wine. "And you have worked far too hard to spend your thirties scraping mud off your boots. You know what things cost, Nora. That is your great advantage over my son. Julian thinks money is something that happens to other people, like bad weather, even as he uses my American Express card to buy his plane tickets to London. You know that a gallon of milk costs four dollars and twenty-nine cents, and you know how long you have to stand on your feet to earn it."

"Three dollars and eighty-nine cents," Nora said automatically. "If you buy the store brand."

Miss Emily smiled—a slow, genuine curving of her thin lips. "There, you see? Priceless." She reached across the tablecloth and patted Nora’s hand. "When the letter comes from Oxford, he will come to you. He won't come to me, because he knows I will tell him to cut two hundred pages about the turnips and put in a chapter about Karl Marx so the undergraduates will have to buy it for their syllabus. Which is what he needs to do. And that is what you will tell him."

"I don't know anything about Karl Marx," Nora said, her heart beating a heavy rhythm against her ribs. "Or turnips."

"You won't say it like that, of course," Miss Emily said, waving a hand dismissively. "You will make him a cup of that dreadful herbal tea he likes, and you will listen to him for an hour, and then you will say, *Darling, perhaps if you opened it up a bit. So more people could see how brilliant it is.* You have a very soothing voice, Nora. He’ll listen to you."

The waiter came to clear the plates. Nora watched his white-gloved hands moving with practiced, invisible efficiency. She knew that movement. It was cousin to the movement she used to make when wiping down the scanner glass with Windex between the five o’clock commuters and the seven o’clock stragglers. Service was service; the only difference was the thickness of the linen and whether or not you were allowed to sit down while you did it.

And what was Miss Emily asking of her, really, except another kind of service? A shift management of the soul, conducted in a pre-war apartment in Riverdale instead of under the humming fluorescents of Lane 4.

When they returned to the Bronxville house late that afternoon, the autumn sun was slanting low through the red oaks. Julian was sitting on the stone terrace at the back of the house, a yellow legal pad balanced on his knee. He had changed his shirt to one that had all its buttons, though the collar was still slightly frayed.

He looked up as the French doors opened and Nora stepped out onto the flagstone. Miss Emily had stayed inside to take a call from Tokyo, leaving Nora carrying the heavy shopping bags.

"You survived," Julian said, smiling up at her, his eyes crinkling behind his wire-rimmed glasses. The relief in his voice was so boyish and unguarded that Nora felt a sharp constriction in her throat. He reached out and took her free hand, pulling her down onto the stone balustrade beside his chair. "Was it terrible? Did she try to make you buy riding boots?"

"She bought me a coat," Nora said, looking down at the top of his head. In the golden light, she could see the pale scalp beneath his soft brown curls. He looked so fragile, sitting there with his fountain pen and his notes on dead farmers, insulated by three generations of compound interest and his mother’s ruthless, unblinking love. "And a dress for the dinner on Thursday."

"You didn't need a new dress," he said, pressing his cheek against her hip, right through the fabric of her old Marshall’s skirt. "I liked the blue one. You looked like yourself in the blue one."

Nora looked back through the glass of the French doors. Deep within the shadows of the drawing room, she could see the silhouette of Miss Emily’s silver hair as she paced behind the sofa, the phone pressed to her ear, her other hand making small, decisive chopping motions in the air as she dismantled someone’s argument six thousand miles away.

Nora looked down at her own right hand, resting on Julian’s shoulder. Automatically, she tucked her thumb into her palm, hiding it beneath her four long fingers. Then, remembering, she slowly drew it out again, laying her hand flat and open against the soft flannel of her husband’s shirt.

"The blue one was polyester, Julian," she said softly, her fingers finding a loose thread at the seam of his collar and pulling it clean. "It didn't breathe. And besides, what are you working on? Tell me about the turnips. Have you ever thought about opening it up a bit?"
